newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria ruler reaffirms army to quit power in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria ruler reaffirms army to quit power in 1998.

text.p: Nigerian military ruler General Sani Abacha has restated his promise that an elected civilian government would be installed in 1998.
Abacha, in a message to an army conference in the northwestern city of Sokoto on Monday, said there was no going back on his transition to civilian rule programme.

It was his first public reaction to growing speculation that he plans to follow the footsteps of army generals in West Africa who have seized power in coup d'etats and then become civilian presidents after holding elections criticised for being unfair.

"It is necessary to state here that the armed forces have no intention to remain in power beyond 1998," Abacha said in the message read on his behalf by the chief of defence staff, Major-General Abdulsalam Abubakar.
"We are firmly committed to the socio-political programme that is on a steady course," he added.
Nigeria has been in crisis since the army annulled a vote in 1993 that would have ended military rule.

Abacha seized power in the mayhem that followed. Since 1994 the undeclared winner of the annulled vote, business mogul Moshood Abiola, has been detained pending trial for treason for proclaiming himself president.
Abacha's critics dismiss his three-year long transition programme as a ruse and insist that he plans to hang onto power into the next century.
"We will not be deterred by the unpatriotic activities and utterances of our detractors who are bent on creating disaffection in the society," he told the army conference.
Five political parties emerged six weeks ago to contest staggered polls beginning next month with local council elections and ending with a presidential vote in 1998.
